'''Saliba''' is an [[Oceanic language]] spoken on the islets off the southeastern tip of [[Papua New Guinea]]. There are approximately 2,500 speakers of Saliba. Significant documentation of the language was undertaken by the Saliba-Logea documentation project, and hundreds of audio-video resources can be found in the project archive.<ref name=":1">Saliba-Logea.  The Language Archive: [http://dobes.mpi.nl/projects/saliba http://dobes.mpi.nl/projects/saliba]</ref>

==Culture==
The most common occupation for the Saliba people is fishing.<ref name=":1" /> The four major villages are Sidudu, Sawasawaga, Logeakai and Logeapwata.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=http://www.sil.org/pacific/png/abstract.asp?id=928474542507|title=Organized Phonology Data of Saliba Language|last1=Oetzel|first1=Sabine|first2=Rainer|last2=Oetzel|date=May 24, 2004|website=SIL|publisher=SIL}}</ref>

===Endangerment===
The Saliba language is currently endangered. Currently there are only elders that speak it and a few young children who have learned in the early years of their life. Most of the people speak English because it is seen as the more prestigious language. This only further makes Saliba the minority language in the land.<ref name=":1" />

==Phonology==
The consonants of Saliba are {{IPA|/b/}}, {{IPA|/bw/}}, {{IPA|/p/}}, {{IPA|/pw/}}, {{IPA|/d/}}, {{IPA|/t/}}, {{IPA|/g/}}, {{IPA|/k/}}, {{IPA|/gw/}}, {{IPA|/kw/}}, {{IPA|/m/}}, {{IPA|/n/}}, {{IPA|/(w)/}}, {{IPA|/(j)/}}, {{IPA|/ ' /}} and {{IPA|/r/}}.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Saliba|last=Mosel|first=Ulrike|publisher=Lincom Europa}}</ref> The vowels of Saliba are {{IPA|/i/}}, {{IPA|/e/}}, {{IPA|/a/}}, {{IPA|/u/}} and {{IPA|/o/}}. The {{IPA|/w/}} and {{IPA|/j/}} are debatable if they are different phonemes because they are in complementary distribution with the sounds {{IPA|/u/}} and {{IPA|/i/}} respectively.<ref name=":0" />

===Syllables===
The syllables in Saliba have three possible structures. They are V, CV, or CVN (CVN being a heavy syllable).  All syllables in Saliba are enunciated the same. There is occasionally a slight stress on the syllable just before the last syllable. For example, in the word {{lang|sbe|la.'pu.i}}, meaning 'hear', the syllable in the middle would be slightly stressed. In Saliba, all nouns, verbs, adjectives, and some adverbs are composed of at least two light syllables or one heavy syllable. On the other hand, words used mostly for grammatical functions, such as conjunctions, pronouns, particles, etc. can be made up of only a CV or just a V.<ref name=":0" />

==Grammar==

===Verbs===
All verbs in Saliba can be classified as either transitive or intransitive verbs on formal grounds. To convert from transitive to intransitive verbs the suffix {{lang|sbe|-i}} or a suffix that looks like {{lang|sbe|-(C)ei}} is used, C being any consonant depending on the verb. The suffix {{lang|sbe|-i}} can also be used to turn some nouns into transitive verbs. For example, {{lang|sbe|nigwa}}, 'knife', becomes {{lang|sbe|nigwa-i}}, 'cut with a knife'. Another important formational affix for verbs is the causative prefix {{lang|sbe|he-}}, e.g. {{lang|sbe|kita}}, 'see' becomes {{lang|sbe|he-kita}}, 'show', or, 'cause to see'. Something special about the verbs in Saliba is that the stems of two lexical verbs can combine to form one inflected verb. For example, in the verb phrase {{lang|sbe|ye-kamposi-dobi}}, which means 'he jumped down', the verb {{lang|sbe|kamposi-dobi}} is made up of {{lang|sbe|kamposi}} ('jump') and {{lang|sbe|dobi}} ('go down'). The two stems have combined to form one complex verb.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Margetts|first=Anna|date=2005|title=Positional Slots In Saliba Complex Verbs|journal=Oceanic Linguistics|volume=44|pages=65–89|doi=10.1353/ol.2005.0023|s2cid=144459254}}</ref>

====Tense and aspect====
Tense is not marked in Saliba verb phrases, but aspect is.<ref name=":0" /> When absolute time reference is needed, Saliba uses time words like {{lang|sbe|lahi}}, 'yesterday', {{lang|sbe|malaitom}}, 'tomorrow', or oblique phrases like {{lang|sbe|malatomtom-yena}}, 'in the morning'.<ref name=":0" />

====Reduplication====
Saliba uses reduplication for a few things. One function of reduplication is to convert certain action verbs into noun. For example, the word {{lang|sbe|kuya}} means 'to sweep'. If {{lang|sbe|kuya}} is reduplicated to {{lang|sbe|kuyakuya}} it becomes 'broom'. Another example could be {{lang|sbe|lau}} meaning 'go'. If that word is reduplicated to {{lang|sbe|laulau}} it now means 'method' or 'way'. Another reason a verb would be reduplicated is the verb is being used as an attributive verb. An example of this would be in the sentence {{lang|sbe|kai namwa-namwa-di}}. That sentence means 'good food'. Notice {{lang|sbe|namwa}}, meaning 'good', is reduplicated since it is a verb that is being used like an adjective. The last reason a verb would get reduplicated is in the imperfective aspect of an action verb. The reduplication is used to mark this occurrence in the sentence. Imperfective aspect is used to show habitual or progressive events. For example, in the sentence {{lang|sbe|...nige koya-i se pai-paisoa}} which means '(they) did not work in the garden'. The {{lang|sbe|pai}} ('work') is reduplicated to mark that this is probably a habitual behavior.<ref name=":0" />

===Adjectives===
As far as adjectives go, in Saliba there appears to be no difference between verbs and adjectives.<ref name=":0" /> The only rule is, with the exception of some verbs, all verbs are duplicated when they are going to be used as adjectives.<ref name=":0" />

===Nouns===
Nouns in Saliba have four kinds of affixes that can be attached to them. The first one is a suffix that is used for possession. The next one is the plural suffix which is ({{lang|sbe|-o}}, {{lang|sbe|-ao}}, {{lang|sbe|-uwo}}, or {{lang|sbe|-wao}}) on nouns that refer to humans. Another affix is the locative suffix ({{lang|sbe|-i}}). The last affix is called a determiner.<ref name=":0" />

====Noun phrases====
Noun phrases are everything in a sentence that is not the verb. Noun phrases can be subjects, objects, predicates and parts of prepositional and post-positional phrases. In its simplest form, a noun phrase can be made out of just a noun and a determiner. For example, {{lang|sbe|mwaedo}}, which in Saliba means 'eel', is a simple noun phrase. A noun phrase is typically broken up into two parts, the nucleus and possibly multiple modifiers. Modifiers can include things like possessors and demonstratives (words that give location), which would go before the head noun. The other types of modifiers, such as verbal modifiers and quantifiers, would go after the head noun.

One of the most important modifiers is the determiner. This modifier is usually attached to the last part of the noun phrase and gives a reference to the head noun in the noun phrase with regard to the rest of the sentence. However, noun phrases used as prepositional phrases do not have determiners.

Quantifiers such as cardinal numerals can go either before or after the adjective in a sentence. Ordinal numerals on the other hand, such as first, second, etc. behave like adjectives and go after the noun in Saliba.<ref name=":0" />

===Possession===
As mentioned previously, Saliba has different rules for possessions depending on if they are alienable possessions or inalienable possessions. If a possession is inalienable, then the possessed noun is written with the correct possessive suffix directly following it, such as {{lang|sbe|sina-gu}}, meaning 'my mother'. {{lang|sbe|-gu}} would be the possessive suffix. However, if it is an alienable possession then the possessive suffix directly follows one of the two possessive classifiers, {{lang|sbe|yo-}} or {{lang|sbe|ka-}}, such as in {{lang|sbe|yo-gu numa}}, 'my house', or {{lang|sbe|ka-gu kai}}, 'my food'. In a sentence the person who possesses the possessed noun is treated as the subject and possessed noun is then the head of the predicate. They are written in such a way that there is nothing separating the subject from the head of the predicate. To negate the predicate, such as saying someone does not have something, the negation particle {{lang|sbe|nige}} would be added before the predicate phrase like so: {{lang|sbe|Yau nige natu-gu}}, meaning 'I don't have a child'. Depending on the context, almost any noun can appear as alienable or inalienable. For example, one could say {{lang|sbe|pou-na}}, meaning 'her egg' (hen's egg), {{lang|sbe|ka-na pou}}, meaning 'his/her egg' (egg that he/she is going to eat), or {{lang|sbe|yo-na pou}}, meaning 'his/her egg' (egg that he/she owns).

The category of ''body parts'' refers to things like hands, feet, etc. ''Parts of inanimate objects'' includes things such as the root of a coconut or the core of an apple. ''Spatial relation'' refers to space, such as the inside of a house. ''Container'' and ''content'' can mean things like a cup of water or a bowl of food. ''Quantity'' and ''quantified'' items are not referring to objects, but are rather more figurative, referring to age and time.<ref name=":0" />

In terms of semantics, linguists can see three different types of relationships based on these constructions. Those relationships are relationships where the possessor and the possessee can part, relationships in which the possessor and the possessee cannot part but the possessor has complete control over the possessee, and a relationship in which the possessor and the possessee cannot part but the possessee has an effect on the possessor. An example of the last relationship would be a body part. Kinship is an outlier and appears in all three categories. Linguists do not know why this is. They can only assume that it is because of historical reasons. Some examples of inalienable kinships and alienable kinships are listed in the following table.<ref name=":0" />

==Basic sentence structure==
Saliba is a [[Subject–object–verb|subject-object-verb]] (SOV) language. Saliba follows the [[Nominative–accusative language|nominative-accusative]] pattern in its sentences. The basic clause in Saliba is composed of a verb with its subject and object with its [[affix]]es. Any noun phrases preceding or succeeding this core can be thought of as an expansion of this clause. A simple sentence could be {{lang|sbe|Kai-wa ka matausi palapa}}, which means 'We were really frightened'. Saliba also has nonverbal clauses such as [[Dependent clause|nominal clauses]], [[existential clause]]s, possessive clauses and clauses with other special predicates.

An example of a nominal clause would be {{lang|sbe|Kita taulauhekata}}, which means 'we are teachers'. The next nonverbal clause is the existential clause. These types of clauses will have the word {{lang|sbe|temenai}} ('there') or a post-positional phrase to refer to a location. An example of this would be in the sentence {{lang|sbe|Temenai sikuli labui}}, which means 'There are two schools'. Another nonverbal clause would be the possessive clause, which is a noun phrase that refers to a possessor and a possessee.<ref name=":0" />

===Determiners===
In Saliba, [[determiner]]s are always the last part of a noun phrase. Most nouns will have a determiner after them. If a noun phrase is a predicate, then it will not have a determiner.<ref name=":0" />

==Particles==
Saliba uses many different particles to mark certain things in sentences. These particles usually go before the verb phrase but there are a couple that can go after the verb phrase.

==={{lang|sbe|Kabo}}===
The particle {{lang|sbe|Kabo}} is used to mark that something new is happening. This could mean a change in the situation, a change in the weather etc. An example sentence would be {{lang|sbe|Ka keno-keno na kabo nabu ye talu}}. This sentence means 'When we were sleeping, it started to rain'. Notice {{lang|sbe|kabo}} is used because something changed, in this case the weather. Another instance in which {{lang|sbe|kabo}} can be used is to indicate an event that will happen in the future. For example, if someone said, "{{lang|sbe|Saha kabo ta ginauli}}", (meaning 'What are we going to do?'), {{lang|sbe|kabo}} is used to imply a change to the current situation. In these examples, {{lang|sbe|kabo}} was used to mark a change but {{lang|sbe|kabo}} can also be used for comparison, such as {{lang|sbe|Maui saliya-na ye loha na kabo Tahali}}, which translates to 'Maui is taller than Tahali'. In all of these sentences the particle is actually placed in many different places in the sentence. For example, in the first sentence the particle was placed before the object, while in the second sentence it was placed before the subject. The placement of this particle varies and there do not appear to be any specific rules as to where to exactly put {{lang|sbe|kabo}} in a sentence. All that is known is that it can sometimes go at the very beginning of a sentence before everything else, just before the subject, or after the subject but before the predicate.<ref name=":0" />

==={{lang|sbe|Bena}}===
This particle is used to mark something that should happen or something that someone should do. The closest English word to this particle would be the word ''must''; however, it is not as strong as ''must''. For example, in the sentence {{lang|sbe|Bena teinamona ku lau maketi}}, which means 'You must go to the market', the particle can be directly translated as 'must'. However, in the following sentence {{lang|sbe|Ya henua bena pasta yo-na pwaole ya kaiwahali}}, meaning 'I want to steal the pastor's rooster', the use of {{lang|sbe|bena}} here is not as strong as something that has to be done, and is closer to 'want' in this case.<ref name=":0" />

==={{lang|sbe|Tabu}}===
{{lang|sbe|Tabu}} is a negation particle. This particle is used when the speaker wants to express something that should not happen or should not be done. For example, in the sentence {{lang|sbe|Tabu ku mode}} the speaker is saying 'don't worry'. Another example with {{lang|sbe|tabu}} is the sentence {{lang|sbe|tabu bena kaitea i kita-gau}}, which means 'Don't let anybody see me'. Note that in the previous sentence, since the subject is third person, the particle {{lang|sbe|tabu}} must be used with the particle {{lang|sbe|bena}} like shown.<ref name=":0" />

==={{lang|sbe|Taba}}===
{{lang|sbe|Taba}} is another negation particle. This particle is used to express something that a person does not want to do. Unlike {{lang|sbe|tabu}} though, {{lang|sbe|taba}} can only be used in conjunction with {{lang|sbe|nige}}, meaning 'not'. An example sentence could be {{lang|sbe|Taba nige ya hedede}}, which means 'I don't want to tell'.<ref name=":0" />

==={{lang|sbe|Besina}}===
{{lang|sbe|Besina}} is a particle that is used to express something that has to be done no matter what. This particle is definitely stronger than {{lang|sbe|bena}} and is probably more closely related to the word ''must'' in English. A way this particle could be used in a sentence is {{lang|sbe|Ye wowolina besina se lau mo}}, which means 'It was stormy but nevertheless they had to go'.<ref name=":0" />

==={{lang|sbe|Gonoana}}===
Linguists cannot classify this particle. They have best described it as an inalienably possessed noun. This particle is used for something that someone is able to do. A simple example would be {{lang|sbe|Gonoa-na u kalina Saliba?}}, meaning 'Can you speak Saliba?'.<ref name=":0" />

==={{lang|sbe|Nuana}}===
The particle {{lang|sbe|nuana}} is used when the speaker is presuming something to be true. For example, the sentence {{lang|sbe|Lahi nuana sina-gu ye lau maketi}}, which means 'Perhaps my mother went to the market yesterday'. As seen in this sentence, {{lang|sbe|nuana}} is used to express the fact that the speaker does not know for sure if his mother went to the market – it is a guess or assumption.<ref name=":0" />

==={{lang|sbe|Yako/ko}}===
These two particles, unlike the ones previously, go after the verb phrase instead of before the verb phrase. Both of these particles are used to express something that has already been done previously before the time at which the speaker is talking about it. The only difference between {{lang|sbe|yako}} and {{lang|sbe|ko}} is that {{lang|sbe|yako}} is used for transitive verb phrases and {{lang|sbe|ko}} is used for intransitive verb phrases. An example sentence using {{lang|sbe|yako}} would be {{lang|sbe|Hewali-wa meta hasala-wa i tawasolao yako}}, which means 'That young man had already married the girl'. An example sentence using {{lang|sbe|ko}} would be {{lang|sbe|Yo-gu numa ye kalasi ko}}, meaning 'My house burnt down'. As shown in both sentences, since these particles go after the verb phrase they are the last things in the sentence.<ref name=":0" />

==={{lang|sbe|Kesegai}}===
This particle, like {{lang|sbe|yako}} and {{lang|sbe|ko}} goes after the verb phrase in the sentence. Clearly this particle is derived from the word {{lang|sbe|kesega}} meaning 'one'. {{lang|sbe|Kesegai}} is used to mark things that happen continuously and without interruption – for example, {{lang|sbe|Nabu ye talu kesegai}}, which means 'It kept on raining'.<ref name=":0" />
